records.title: Adoption of biosecurity practices on dairy farms: a systematic review of barriers and facilitators
records.authors: Van Rensburg-Okoli T, Brannigan-Sato M, Holmqvist-Adeyemi R
records.venue: Journal of Farm Animal Health Management
records.abstract: We reviewed 41 studies of biosecurity practice on dairy farms in temperate countries. Fewer than half of farms reported isolating purchased cattle, and footbath use, visitor controls and vehicle hygiene varied widely. Barriers most often reported were cost, time, farm layout and a belief that disease comes from neighbours rather than purchases. Facilitators were advice tailored to the farm, a trusted veterinarian and visible disease events nearby. Only six studies evaluated an intervention to increase adoption, and most measured practices by farmer report rather than observation.

records.title: Quarantine of purchased cattle on dairy farms: a cross-sectional survey of 312 herds
records.abstract: We surveyed 312 dairy herds in two regions about how purchased cattle were introduced. Thirty-four percent of herds that had bought cattle in the previous year kept them apart from the main herd for at least three weeks, and 12 percent tested them before mixing. Larger herds and herds with a written herd health plan quarantined more often. Farmers who did not quarantine most often cited lack of separate housing and labour at busy times. The survey relied on farmer report and had a response of 44 percent.

records.title: Veterinary-facilitated biosecurity planning and adoption of measures on dairy farms: a cluster-randomised trial in 60 herds
records.authors: O'Donovan-Mbeki C, Lundgren-Asante E, Tamura-Fitzgerald H
records.abstract: Sixty dairy herds served by four practices were randomly allocated by practice to a facilitated biosecurity planning visit, in which the herd's own veterinarian agreed three farm-specific priorities with the farmer, or to usual advice. At 12 months, observed adoption rose by a mean of 2.1 of 12 measures in planning herds against 0.8 in usual-advice herds. The difference was largest for isolation of purchased cattle and visitor controls. Visits took a median of 2.5 hours including follow-up. Effects at 24 months were not measured.

records.title: Why the advice stays on the shelf: interviews with dairy farmers about biosecurity
records.abstract: We interviewed 28 dairy farmers about the biosecurity advice they had received. Most described advice as generic lists that did not fit their buildings or workload. Farmers trusted their own veterinarian more than leaflets or campaigns, but said advice was rarely followed up. Measures were adopted when they solved a problem the farmer had already seen, such as an outbreak on the farm or nearby. Several farmers said they would act on two or three priorities agreed for their farm but not on a list of fifteen.

records.title: Measuring biosecurity on dairy farms: agreement between farmer-reported and observed practices
records.abstract: On 85 dairy farms, a researcher observed 10 biosecurity practices during an unannounced visit after the farmer had completed a questionnaire about the same practices. Farmers reported isolating purchased cattle on 61 percent of farms, but isolation facilities in use were observed on 29 percent. Agreement was good for footbath presence but poor for footbath use and visitor controls. The authors recommend observed measures for evaluating biosecurity interventions and note that unannounced visits were acceptable to most farmers. Observation took about 40 minutes per farm, and two farmers declined the unannounced visit.

response.synthesis: Five retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; the search returned few hits. Biosecurity adoption on dairy farms is low, with isolation of purchased cattle practised by about a third of herds that buy stock. One cluster-randomised trial found that a vet-facilitated plan with three farm-specific priorities raised observed adoption more than usual advice, and farmers describe acting on a few agreed priorities rather than generic lists. Farmer report overstates practice, so adoption must be observed.
response.gradeRationale: One moderate-quality trial in volunteer practices supports facilitated planning; the rest is observational or qualitative with self-report bias and indirectness to this practice.
response.summary: Five retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; overall certainty low.

response.overview: Implementation study in one veterinary practice: facilitated biosecurity planning visits for consenting client dairy herds, with observed adoption of five core measures at baseline and six months and a record of how visits were delivered.
response.population: Client dairy herds of the practice whose farmers give written agreement; herds under a disease-control restriction at baseline are excluded until it is lifted.
response.exposure: One facilitated planning visit by the herd's own vet (about two hours), agreeing three farm-specific priorities from five core measures (isolation of purchased cattle, visitor controls, footbath use, vehicle hygiene, boundary contact), with a follow-up call at six weeks.
response.procedures: At baseline a second vet observes the five measures during an unannounced visit. The herd's vet then holds the planning visit using a short structured guide and records the priorities agreed. The follow-up call checks progress. At six months the observing vet repeats the unannounced visit. Delivery is recorded with a fidelity checklist; farmers rate acceptability on a five-point scale.

response.theoreticalFramework: RE-AIM to organise reach, adoption, implementation fidelity and maintenance; it earns its place because the question is delivery.
response.summary: Implementation study with observed adoption as the primary outcome and fidelity, reach and vet time recorded.

response.designSummary: Before-after comparison within participating herds of observed core measures, with implementation outcomes described.
response.sampleSize: About 20 herds can be served with the vet time available. With a standard deviation of about 1.2 measures in the change from baseline, 20 herds give a 95 percent confidence interval of about 0.55 measures either side of the mean change, enough to tell a change of 1.5 from no change. The number of client dairy herds has not been stated, so reach cannot yet be projected.
response.primaryAnalysis: Mean change in the number of observed core measures from baseline to six months with a 95 percent confidence interval (paired analysis).
response.secondaryAnalysis: Adoption of each measure; delivery fidelity; reach by herd size and tenure; vet time per herd; farmer acceptability.
response.missingData: Herds that leave before six months are described; the primary analysis uses herds observed at both visits, with a sensitivity analysis counting missing follow-up as no change.
response.summary: About 20 herds give an interval of about half a measure around the mean change.

response.risks: Low: farmers give time and allow observation; no procedures on animals beyond usual care. Risks are loss of trust if observation feels like inspection, and confidentiality of disease status.
response.consent: Written agreement from each farmer, covering the planning visit and unannounced observation visits, with the right to withdraw at any time.
response.data: Farm names are replaced by codes in the analysis file; disease information is not shared outside the practice.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus adapted to farms: small, tenant and family farms with little spare housing or labour, older farmers and farm workers with limited English may benefit less. Reach and adoption are reported by herd size and tenure, and priorities include low-cost measures.
response.effectiveness: Useful if observed adoption rises and the practice can see what delivery costs in vet time.
response.costs: About 50 vet half-days over six months; no equipment purchase by farmers.
response.grants: None; a positive result could support an application to a regional animal health fund.
response.partnerships: Practice vets, two farmer partners from the practice's client group, and the regional milk buyer's advisory team for dissemination.
response.rebPath: The practice will ask the veterinary school's human research ethics committee whether farmer participation needs review; no animal procedures are involved, so animal ethics approval is not required. ICH-GCP principles are followed for consent.
response.limitations: Few herds, one practice, no concurrent comparison, six-month follow-up only.
response.summary: Low-risk study with farmer consent, confidentiality of disease status and equity attention to small and tenant farms.

response.partnershipPlan: Two farmer partners from the client group review the planning guide and the observation checklist; a farm worker reviews the visitor-control wording.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; comments from the practice's client evenings are summarised.

response.title: Facilitated biosecurity planning in client dairy herds of one veterinary practice: an implementation study
response.abstract: Aim: to assess whether facilitated biosecurity planning visits by the herd's own vet can be delivered in routine practice and are followed by adoption of observed core measures. Methods: implementation study in consenting client dairy herds, January to June 2027, with unannounced observation of five measures at baseline and six months and a delivery fidelity record. Results and conclusions will be written after follow-up.
response.introduction: Biosecurity advice is often not followed on dairy farms, and farmer report overstates practice. A randomised trial showed that facilitated plans with a few farm-specific priorities raise observed adoption; whether a single practice can deliver them is unknown.
response.methods: Each herd received one planning visit agreeing three priorities and a follow-up call. A second vet observed five core measures unannounced at baseline and six months. Delivery, reach and vet time were recorded.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present reach, delivery fidelity, change in observed measures and vet time per herd.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret adoption in light of delivery and reach and describe what the practice would need to sustain visits.
response.limitations: Few herds, no concurrent comparison, volunteer farms and short follow-up.
